models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because the two signals carry very different information at the industry level.

For value, cross-industry comparisons of ratios like book-to-price are mostly noise. Industries differ structurally in accounting conventions, capital intensity, intangibles, leverage and growth prospects, so a "cheap" industry is usually not mispriced, just different. Betting on cheap industries therefore earns little or no premium, yet it adds a lot of risk: concentrated, persistent sector exposures (for example long financials and energy, short tech) that are volatile and prone to crashes. Removing industry bets strips out uncompensated risk while keeping the within-industry comparison, where value ratios are comparable and do predict returns. The Sharpe ratio rises markedly (Cohen and Polk; Asness, Porter and Stevens; Novy-Marx).

For momentum, the industry component is itself a priced signal. Moskowitz and Grinblatt (1999) showed that industry momentum is strong and accounts for a substantial part of stock-level momentum. Past returns are also directly comparable across industries, unlike accounting ratios. So industry-neutralising momentum reduces risk but also gives up real return, leaving only a modest net improvement.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Removing industry bets helps value much more because value's industry component adds a lot of risk and earns almost nothing, while momentum's industry component actually pays.

**Value.** Valuation ratios differ across industries for lasting structural reasons, such as accounting conventions, capital intensity, growth prospects and leverage. A utility or bank will nearly always look "cheaper" on book-to-price than a software firm, and that gap mostly doesn't close. As a result, a raw value portfolio ends up with large, persistent industry tilts. Those tilts add a lot of correlated volatility and have historically earned little premium, since industry-level value is a weak predictor of returns (Asness, Porter and Stevens 2000). Ranking stocks against their own industry peers keeps the part that does predict returns, a stock being mispriced relative to similar firms, and drops the unrewarded noise. Volatility falls a lot while returns hold up or improve, so the Sharpe ratio rises sharply.

**Momentum.** Industry momentum is a real, rewarded effect (Moskowitz and Grinblatt 1999). Momentum's industry tilts also rotate over time rather than being stuck in the same sectors. Neutralizing industries therefore removes some genuine return along with the risk, so the net gain is modest.

Removing industry bets dramatically improves value strategies because valuation multiples are not directly comparable across industries. Structural differences in accounting rules, capital intensity, intangible assets, and growth profiles cause certain sectors—like utilities or financials—to appear persistently cheap while others—like technology or healthcare—appear persistently expensive. An unconstrained value portfolio therefore takes large, static industry bets that add substantial volatility without commensurate expected returns. Neutralizing industry exposure strips out this structural noise, ensuring the strategy compares apples to apples and isolates genuine relative mispricing among true peers.

Momentum, by contrast, relies on past returns, which are inherently comparable across industries and unaffected by accounting conventions. More importantly, industry momentum is itself a well-documented source of alpha driven by slow information diffusion and investor underreaction to sector-wide economic shocks. While industry-neutralizing momentum can modestly reduce volatility, it also discards a genuinely rewarded component of the signal. In short, industry bets represent mostly uncompensated structural noise in value, whereas they carry meaningful return-predicting information in momentum.

Value ratios are more informative when you compare companies in the same industry. A utility can look cheap next to a software company because the two industries differ in growth prospects, capital needs, and how they account for assets. A value strategy that ranks both together can end up making large industry bets on the basis of those structural differences. Removing industry bets lets the strategy focus on which companies are cheap relative to their peers.

Momentum gets part of its predictive power from industry moves. When investors revise their expectations for an entire industry, stocks in that industry can rise or fall together for months. Removing industry bets can reduce concentration risk, but it also strips out some of the return signal.
